summary: Weekly POC check-in focusing on prefix and KV cache hit rates and prompt reuse strategy. Reviewed recent benchmark results: end-to-end median latency improved with caching but tail latency and cold-start miss rates persist. Discussed key-normalization, TTL tuning, and tradeoffs between larger prefix keys vs smaller hashed keys. Agreed on experiments: increase TTL, normalize prompts to reduce variance, run targeted burst tests on Dedicated node, and share sanitized logs for further analysis.
topics: Current hit rate metrics and interpretation
TTL and cache eviction policy experiments
Benchmark setup for burst testing and Dedicated node
Security and data handling for prompt logs
transcript:
00:00 Alex Turner: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we good to start?
00:07 Daniel Kim: Yeah, thanks Alex, we got a full house here. Quick note, running from 15:00-15:40 our side.
00:13 Priya Shah: cool, i'll share my screen in a sec, got the dashboard up — showing prefix/KV cache hit rates.
00:21 Sofia Reyes: great, we've been watching the dashboard, interesting to see the variance day-to-day.
00:30 Priya Shah: ok, so last week we ran the TTL bump to 10 minutes, and as you can see overall KV hit rate moved from ~38% to ~54%. that's median, but tail is still rough — p95 still shows a lot of misses.
00:46 Martin Li: p95 meaning 95th percentile end to end or just cache lookup?
00:51 Priya Shah: good point — here p95 is end-to-end response, but we also have internal metrics showing cache lookup p95 miss ratio. there's a gap when new sessions come in with slightly different prompt prefixes.
01:05 Daniel Kim: that's the problem we're seeing — front-end micro prompts include session metadata, timestamps, small IDs, so they don't reuse prefixes well.
01:13 Alex Turner: right, so one axis is normalizing prompts before cache keying. second is TTL. third is key construction — whether we use long prefix strings or hashed normalized keys.
01:24 Sofia Reyes: can you run through what normalization would mean concretely? we worry about losing intent if we strip too much.
01:30 Priya Shah: totally — in practice we propose token-level normalization: strip session ids, lower-case, collapse whitespace, optionally replace numeric IDs with <ID> placeholder. we keep semantic tokens that are important like 'diagnose' or 'prescribe'.
01:45 Daniel Kim: hmm, that could work. but our logs include PHI-ish tokens — would normalization need to be done in-customer before sending to Redwood?
01:53 Alex Turner: yes, we strongly recommend doing customer-side sanitization for any PHI. for the POC you can provide anonymized logs — the sandbox can show patterns without exposing PHI.
02:03 Martin Li: ok we'll get S about that. Sofia, can you handle redacting and uploading a week?
02:09 Sofia Reyes: yes i can. got it.
02:12 Priya Shah: back to hit rates — after normalization in our sim we saw hit rate improve another ~12 points, so combined TTL+norm got us into the 65-70% range on median. but again, cold start sequences and rare prompts still miss.
02:27 Alex Turner: what's the cost delta for your workload with that hit rate? did you see token cost changes?
02:33 Priya Shah: roughly 18% lower token cost per request averaged, because caching avoids re-run of the entire prefix through the model. CPU also lowers. we can share the budget spreadsheet.
02:42 Daniel Kim: that's promising. we need to understand tail latency. Our SLAs are sensitive; p99 above 2 seconds is hard.
02:49 Priya Shah: agreed — tail is where we need to focus. some of the misses are due to very small variations — timestamps, trailing punctuation. key-normalization helps but we also want a fallback routing policy: if cache miss, route to a cheaper model variant or different cluster to prevent overloads.
03:05 Martin Li: can Redwood do automatic fallback to cheaper model variant? we were talking about cost leakage if we route all misses to the big model.
03:11 Alex Turner: yes, routing policy is configurable — can route by latency budget, cost budget, or region. during the POC we can set up a canary that routes up to X% of misses to the large model and rest to a slightly smaller model, to maintain latency.
03:23 Sofia Reyes: ok, and can the KV cache be replicated across Dedicated nodes? because our infra has multiple regions and we don't want cross-region misses adding latency.
03:31 Priya Shah: currently we can do regional caches with sticky routing. cross-region replication is planned but not enabled for this POC. recommended is co-locating dedicated nodes or using per-region caches.
03:41 Daniel Kim: that adds complexity for us, but probably manageable. about the experiments — what exactly are you proposing next week?
03:47 Priya Shah: short list: 1) increase TTL to 30 minutes for stable prefixes and monitor freshness issues, 2) implement client-side normalization (we'll provide recommended regexes), 3) run a burst test on a transient Dedicated node to observe tail under load, 4) collect sanitized logs for deeper prefix analysis.
04:05 Alex Turner: we should discuss guardrails — TTL increases can lead to stale context if prompts rely on recent state. need product owners to sign off.
04:12 Aisha Chowdhury: from product perspective, 30 minutes seems long. some flows rely on recent user state, but maybe we can scope which endpoints use longer TTL?
04:21 Priya Shah: yes, TTL is per-route. you can keep low TTL for transactional routes and longer one for common FAQ-style prompts.
04:28 Daniel Kim: makes sense. question on key size — Priya you mentioned hashing normalized prompt vs storing full prefix in KV key. tradeoffs?
04:34 Priya Shah: hashing reduces key storage and avoids excessive key length issues, but then you need to ensure your normalization function is collision-resistant for the expected distribution. storing full prefix helps debugging but can increase memory overhead. We typically hash if the prefix length > 256 chars.
04:52 Martin Li: any implications for compliance or audit logs if we hash keys? we need to trace back responses during incidents.
04:58 Alex Turner: you can store hashes plus a separate, short, encrypted summary for audit that contains a redacted prefix. we can integrate with your KMS for that.
05:07 Sofia Reyes: ok good. about the simulation results — can you share the raw metrics? concurrency, qps, token distribution?
05:13 Priya Shah: yes, attached in the spreadsheet I'll share — median RTT, p95, p99, KV hit rate, percent of requests that hit prefix cache vs KV, token counts etc. note that our sample set excludes outliers where input was >1024 tokens.
05:26 Daniel Kim: are there any algorithmic suggestions for improving reuse beyond normalization? like prompt templating or client-side caching?
05:32 Priya Shah: templating helps a lot — if you can move variable pieces into structured fields and keep the semantic prefix consistent, hit rates jump. client-side caching for repeated identical prompts is also useful for immediate repeats.
05:43 Alex Turner: another trick is response chunking and streaming; if prefix is expensive but identical, you can precompute some partial KV and stream the rest. depends on your UX.
05:52 Aisha Chowdhury: one more: how does this affect evaluation and model drift? if we're serving cached outputs based on older model, could that cause quality regressions on rollouts?
05:59 Priya Shah: excellent question — Redwood ties caching TTL to model version. when you roll a new model, you can invalidate caches for routes tied to that model or set a short warm-up period. We recommend canarying and auto-invalidating cache when model version changes to avoid stale responses.
06:14 Daniel Kim: perfect. any security review items? we had asked about KMS and audit logs last week.
06:19 Alex Turner: quick recap — Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest and can push audit logs to your SIEM. For the POC we'll keep logs in the sandbox but we'll provide examples for integration.
06:29 Martin Li: good, that covers the compliance checklist for now.
06:33 Priya Shah: next up I want to show a small chart comparing normalized vs raw hit rate — hang on, sharing.
06:40 [screen share noises, brief pause]
07:05 Priya Shah: ok on the chart you can see raw prefix hit 38% -> TTL 10 min -> 54% -> add normalization -> 66%. p99 latency improved from 3.8s to 2.6s but still above your 2s SLA.
07:20 Daniel Kim: so still need to shave off ~0.6s at tail. any ideas?
07:25 Priya Shah: couple options: more aggressive normalization + more routing to smaller models for misses, or increase parallelism on our serving runtime to reduce queuing for cold misses. the latter is infra-heavy.
07:38 Sofia Reyes: could we also pre-warm cache for top N prefixes based on logs?
07:42 Priya Shah: yes — pre-warm for top 1000 prefixes nightly is a very common pattern and helps p99. we'll provide a script to compute top prefixes and a pre-warm API to load them.
07:53 Alex Turner: timeline wise, I'd say next 2 weeks we can show improved p99 with pre-warm + TTL + normalization. need your sanitized logs to compute top prefixes.
08:02 Daniel Kim: i'll push for the log share, but need to get legal signoff.
08:06 Aisha Chowdhury: i'll coordinate with legal; we'll aim to have redacted logs ready by Friday.
08:11 Priya Shah: great, I'll put together the regexes for normalization and the details of the experiments.
08:15 Alex Turner: ok any blockers?
08:18 Martin Li: just the legal for logs and permission to provision a transient Dedicated node for the burst test.
08:24 Alex Turner: we can keep the Dedicated node ephemeral — one-off for the benchmark, we'll handle provisioning and teardown.
08:30 Daniel Kim: fine. what's the plan for measuring success? specific metrics?
08:34 Priya Shah: primary KPIs: KV/prefix hit rate (median and p95), p99 end-to-end latency, token cost per 1k requests, and percentage of requests routed to fallback model. We'll aim for p99 < 2s and token cost reduction >= 15% as success criteria for this phase.
08:52 Sofia Reyes: sounds reasonable. can you also document experiment config in a single place? we want reproducibility.
08:57 Priya Shah: yes, we'll push a shared doc with exact TTLs, normalization regexes, key hashing choices, routing rules and how to reproduce the bench.
09:05 Alex Turner: quick recap and next steps — (1) Alex to send config + spreadsheet by Friday, (2) Nimbus to share sanitized logs by Friday, (3) Priya to run TTL+norm experiment and share detailed metrics next Tue, (4) schedule Dedicated burst test next week pending infra approvals. Anything else?
09:25 Daniel Kim: nothing from me, thanks.
09:27 Aisha Chowdhury: thanks everyone.
09:30 Alex Turner: thanks team, we'll follow up in thread. Bye.
09:33 [call end]
